extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors and litigators drafting or defending AI/software patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and evaluating patent specifications and claims for AI/software inventions to satisfy 35 U.S.C. §112 written description, enablement, and definiteness (means-plus-function) requirements. Emphasizes what to disclose in the specification and how courts treat sparse/black-box disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: §112(a) written description and enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must provide a 'written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an inventor 'claims a lot but describes or enables a little,' the claims can be invalidated (Bonito Boats; Amgen). Courts invalidate AI-related claims that recite features without sufficient detail about operation and function (Impact Engine v. Google). Enablement/written description failures can result from disclosing only certain examples while claiming a broader genus (Amgen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid black-boxing AI features (generic 'machine learning'/'neural networks')
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite AI-related features merely as 'machine learning', 'deep learning', 'neural network', or other high-level terms without elaborating implementation details risk §112 invalidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Impact Engine’s 'compiler' described only as a box in a figure was insufficient. Listing terms like 'reinforcement learning' or 'semi-supervised learning' without substantive disclosure can render claims non-enabled (hypothetical Claim 2 analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus-species enablement risk post-Amgen
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification that discloses only certain examples may not enable an entire claimed genus; under Amgen, failure to enable the full scope of claims can invalidate genus claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amgen emphasized that disclosing only certain examples can force a POSITA into 'painstaking experimentation' to make other embodiments. Courts may be more willing to challenge broad genus claims after Amgen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration but limits of POSITA knowledge for §112(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person of ordinary skill in the art’s (POSITA) knowledge can be considered and may support written description and enablement when supported by credible evidence and expert testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as Streck, Eli Lilly, Centripetal (jury credited expert identification of specification passages) and Masimo show POSITA knowledge can help, but courts give little weight to unsupported assertions (In re Starrett). POSITA knowledge is not dispositive if unsupported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (§112(b), §112(f)) coverage limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Means-plus-function claim elements are limited to the 'means ... or the equivalent of the structures, material, or acts described in the patent specification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WMS Gaming; drafters may be tempted to use means-plus-function to avoid specificity, but doing so limits the claim to structures actually disclosed (and equivalents) in the spec and risks narrow construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software corresponding-structure requirement: step-by-step algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: For software means-plus-function claims, the corresponding structure cannot be a general-purpose computer; special programming or a step-by-step algorithm must be disclosed as the corresponding structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ergo Licensing/CareFusion requires disclosure of an algorithm when special programming is required. Courts have invalidated claims where only a general-purpose computer or an abstraction was cited as structure (Aristocrat; Ergo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Impermissible black-box algorithms under §112(b,f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosing only inputs and outputs or naming an abstract component (an 'access control manager', 'compiler', etc.) without a concrete algorithm is insufficient for §112(b,f) and renders the claim indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Augme Technologies (no algorithm beyond inputs/outputs), Blackboard (access control manager = black box), and Finisar (rephrasing function) show courts demand algorithmic detail rather than functional restatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot rely on POSITA knowledge to supply algorithm for means-plus-function
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee cannot substitute a POSITA’s knowledge for disclosure of structure/algorithm required by §112(b,f); relying on what a skilled artisan could devise is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackboard and Medical Instrumentation cases: it is improper to look to POSITA knowledge 'apart from and unconnected to the disclosure of the patent.' Ibormeith invalidated an AI drowsiness-detection patent for overreliance on POSITA knowledge without specification of factor weighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic 'software' language and verbs like 'analyzing'/'processing' are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic references to 'software' or functional verbs (e.g., 'analyzing', 'processing') without step-by-step disclosure do not satisfy algorithm/structure requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finisar and Napco explain that merely saying 'software 132 (executed by CPU 130) ... generates ... indices' or using 'analyzing' is an abstraction/rephrasing of function and not an algorithmic disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional source code must be demonstrably operational
rubrics_metrics.description: Citing actual source code may satisfy algorithm disclosure requirements, but the code must be functional and demonstrably implement the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Media Rights Tech. v. Capital One, cited C++ code was non-functional and therefore insufficient; expert testimony showed the code only returned error messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose training data, network attributes, algorithms, and techniques where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications for AI inventions should describe specific algorithms, training datasets, neural network attributes (layers, activation functions, weights, biases), and training techniques to enable reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article advises that details like activation functions, weights, biases, training data and techniques help satisfy §112(a); absence of those details risks undue experimentation and invalidity (discussion in hypothetical and takeaways).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide credible expert testimony and extrinsic evidence when relying on state-of-the-art knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: If a specification relies in part on technologies that were well-known at the priority date, patentees should document or present credible expert testimony and evidence confirming that such technologies were known to a POSITA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may uphold validity when a POSITA-expert ties specification disclosures to known techniques (Centripetal, Masimo). In re Starrett shows conclusory assertions without evidence will fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting broad machine-learning methods without detail likely non-enabled
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming that a module uses 'semi-supervised learning' or 'reinforcement learning' without describing how to implement those methods can cover more embodiments than the specification enables and lead to invalidation under §112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothetical Claim 2: reciting reinforcement/semi-supervised learning without details presents the same problems as Starrett and Amgen — a POSITA would need undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function scope may be limited to specification disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if algorithmic detail is provided, means-plus-function limitations risk being construed to the particular structures and algorithms disclosed in the specification, narrowing claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Takeaway: disclosing details can save claims from indefiniteness but may tighten their scope to the disclosed implementations (risk of limiting effect of means-plus-function claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary practical remedy: comprehensive, detailed specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary cure for §112(a) and §112(b,f) issues in AI/software patents is a detailed specification that discloses how the invention works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article conclusion: despite drafting difficulty, patentees should disclose step-by-step algorithms, training data/techniques, network attributes, and evidence of operation where feasible. 'Today's case may involve a new technology, but the legal principle is the same.' (Amgen)
